answers.primary: A PreToolUse hook registered in managed policy settings, matching Edit|Write|Bash (and the PowerShell tool), that inspects tool_input and returns hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision "deny" (or exits 2) for any path or command string touching secrets/. Back it with permissions.deny rules such as Edit(./secrets/**), Read(./secrets/**) and Bash deny patterns, since deny rules are evaluated by the harness in every permission mode including bypassPermissions and auto mode.
answers.rejected_alternative: A CLAUDE.md rule (or a stated conversational boundary) telling Claude never to touch secrets/ - the docs are explicit that a conversational boundary is re-read from the transcript and can be lost to compaction, so it is not the hard guarantee compliance is asking for.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Both the permission-rule evaluator and the PreToolUse hook run outside the model's control loop; the model never sees a choice, the tool call is refused before execution and only the denial reason is returned to it.
answers.context_boundary: The hook executes in its own OS process with the tool-call JSON on stdin, so the matching logic never occupies the session context window. Only the short permissionDecisionReason string crosses back into the conversation, which is also what the model would use to reason about a workaround.
answers.lifecycle: Fires on every matching tool call for the whole session, from the first tool use until the session ends; it applies regardless of permission mode and cannot be switched off mid-session. Placing it in managed policy settings with allowManagedHooksOnly stops a developer removing it from user or project settings.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed on the tool call, but the Bash surface is the weak spot: prefix-style deny patterns are trivially evaded by indirection (variables, command substitution, symlinks, a helper script), so the hook must normalise and inspect the actual command text rather than trust a glob. If the hook script itself errors with a code other than 2 the call is treated as a non-blocking error and execution continues, so the script must default to deny on parse failure.
answers.version_caveat: Only exit code 2 blocks; exit 1 is non-blocking. Hooks run without a controlling terminal as of v2.1.139, so they cannot write to /dev/tty. Managed policy settings with allowManagedHooksOnly (and permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode) are the enterprise-plan controls that make this non-overridable; deny and ask rules apply in every mode, while allow rules are the ones dropped under bypassPermissions.

answers.primary: A project skill at .claude/skills/release/SKILL.md, with the 400 ordered steps split into on-demand reference files in the skill directory and the two helper scripts shipped alongside and invoked by path rather than pasted inline. Only the skill's name and description sit in context at startup; the body loads when Claude invokes it or the operator types /release.
answers.rejected_alternative: Putting the runbook in CLAUDE.md - CLAUDE.md content is injected as a user message on every session regardless of relevance, which is exactly the per-conversation token cost the team is objecting to.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The harness only surfaces the skill's metadata and loads the body on request; whether the runbook is followed, and followed in order, is the model's decision.
answers.context_boundary: Runs in the main session context. At startup only the frontmatter description crosses in; the SKILL.md body crosses in when triggered, and each reference file only when the model reads it. Helper scripts run as subprocesses, so only their stdout enters context, not their source.
answers.lifecycle: Triggered by the model matching the description to the task, or by the human typing /release; it stops applying when the release conversation ends. It is reloaded per session from disk, so edits take effect on the next session with no install step.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open. The usual failures are a vague description so the model never loads the skill (the runbook silently does not happen), and step-skipping or reordering on a 400-line procedure once it is loaded. Enforce the irreversible steps with hooks or permission rules rather than trusting the prose.
answers.version_caveat: Custom commands were merged into skills, so an existing .claude/commands/release.md still works and produces the same /release, but only the skills/ directory layout gives you the supporting-file directory and the invocation-control frontmatter. Claude Code skills follow the Agent Skills open standard, with Claude-Code-only extensions such as subagent execution and dynamic context injection.

answers.primary: An MCP server for the tracker, added with the HTTP transport (claude mcp add --transport http tracker https://tracker.internal/mcp) at project scope so the entry lives in the repo's .mcp.json, with each developer completing the browser OAuth flow once via /mcp then selecting Authenticate.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill that shells out to the tracker's REST API with curl - it would work, but it pushes token storage, refresh and OAuth callback handling into a script instead of using the transport layer that already handles them.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the connection, the OAuth handshake and token storage, and gates the first tool call behind a permission prompt. The model owns when to call a tool and what to write back into a ticket.
answers.context_boundary: Runs in the main session context, but the server's tool schemas and server instructions are loaded into every session's context window whether used or not. Across the boundary go the tool arguments the model emits and the JSON results the server returns; the OAuth token never enters context.
answers.lifecycle: Connects at session start when Claude Code reads .mcp.json, and each new teammate gets a one-time approval prompt for the project-scoped server. It stops at session end; the OAuth grant persists until it expires or is revoked, at which point the server reverts to "Needs authentication".
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed and loudly: an expired grant or unreachable host shows "Needs authentication" or "Failed to connect" and the tools simply are not offered, so Claude falls back to asking the human, which is the pasting behaviour you were removing. The quieter cost is context: a chatty tracker server's tool definitions consume window on every turn.
answers.version_caveat: .mcp.json is read once at session start, so edits need a restart, and a previously rejected server needs claude mcp reset-project-choices. Startup times out at 30s unless MCP_TIMEOUT is raised. From v2.1.191 a 404 names the URL it tried. Consider MCP tool search to defer tool definitions, and managed MCP policy settings if the org needs to allowlist servers.

answers.primary: A SessionStart hook of type "command" in the repo's .claude/settings.json, matched on startup|resume|clear|compact, that shells out to the tracker CLI and git, and returns hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext containing the sprint ticket list and the current branch.
answers.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md - it is the right home for static project facts and loads automatically, but it cannot execute anything, so it can never carry a sprint list that is correct at the moment the session opens.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code runs the hook before the first turn and splices its stdout into the conversation; the model does not choose whether the context arrives.
answers.context_boundary: The hook process runs entirely outside the context window with the session JSON on stdin. Only the additionalContext string crosses in, at the start of the conversation, so keep it to a compact list rather than a full API dump.
answers.lifecycle: Runs at session start and again on resume, /clear, compaction and forks, per the matcher you set. The injected text is an ordinary early conversation turn, so it goes stale as the session runs and can be dropped by compaction unless the compact matcher re-injects it.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and silently. SessionStart cannot block, so if the tracker is down or the credential has expired the session starts anyway with no sprint context and nothing tells the user - the model then confidently works from nothing. It also puts a network round trip on the critical path of every single session start, so it must be fast and time-bounded.
answers.version_caveat: SessionStart supports only the command and mcp_tool handler types, not http, prompt or agent. Its other output fields (initialUserMessage, sessionTitle, watchPaths, reloadSkills) are available on the same event. Hooks run without a controlling terminal from v2.1.139, so the script must not try to prompt.

answers.primary: One plugin containing skills/ for the code-review helper, hooks/hooks.json for the lifecycle automations and .mcp.json for the tracker integration, published through a private git marketplace and pinned with an explicit version field in .claude-plugin/plugin.json. Each consuming repo declares extraKnownMarketplaces and enabledPlugins in its .claude/settings.json, or the org pushes both through managed settings so it installs at managed scope.
answers.rejected_alternative: Standalone .claude/ configuration copied into all 40 repos - it works for one project but has no version handle and no update path, so shipping a fix means 40 pull requests.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns discovery, installation, versioning and loading of the bundle. Ownership of the individual outcomes then splits: the hooks are harness-enforced, the code-review skill is model-invoked and advisory.
answers.context_boundary: The plugin's components load into each consuming session's own context. Skill descriptions and the MCP server's tool definitions cost window every turn (the /plugin detail view shows a Context cost estimate); hook logic runs out-of-context in its own process.
answers.lifecycle: Loads at session start once installed and enabled, and reloads on /reload-plugins. Consumers move to a new version when you bump plugin.json version and their marketplace auto-update runs (checked after session start with up to a ten-minute jitter, so the running session keeps its loaded version).
answers.failure_mode: Fails open at the distribution layer, which is the real risk at 40 repos: a plugin that only a project settings.json enables and that comes from an external source does not load until the team member actually installs it, and Claude Code just reports it as not installed. Skew is the steady-state problem - some repos on old versions, some never reloaded - so treat managed settings as the only path if you need a guarantee rather than a nudge.
answers.version_caveat: Omitting version makes the git commit SHA the version, so every commit counts as an update; set it explicitly. The per-load install requirement is v2.1.195+; "Will install" component listing is v2.1.145+, context cost v2.1.143+, last-updated v2.1.144+. Admins can set autoUpdate on each extraKnownMarketplaces entry and restrict sources with strictKnownMarketplaces. Plugin skills are namespaced /plugin-name:skill-name.

answers.primary: A skill (deploy) whose frontmatter sets disable-model-invocation: true, so it is excluded from the model-invocable toolkit and exists only as the slash command /deploy that a human types. The ordered procedure and any helper scripts live in the skill directory.
answers.rejected_alternative: A subagent for deploys - it packages the procedure just as well, but the main agent can spawn one on its own judgement, which is precisely the trigger condition you are trying to remove.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split. The harness enforces the entry point: with disable-model-invocation set, the skill is not offered to the model and it cannot invoke it. The model owns everything after the human types the command.
answers.context_boundary: Main session context. Nothing of the skill body crosses in until the human invokes it; then the SKILL.md body plus any $ARGUMENTS enter context and the helper scripts run as subprocesses whose stdout comes back.
answers.lifecycle: Starts only on an explicit human /deploy in the interactive session, and stops applying when that turn's procedure completes. It is not reachable from a subagent's or a teammate's own reasoning.
answers.failure_mode: The gate is hard but narrow, so it fails open around the edges: nothing stops the model from running the underlying kubectl/terraform/deploy commands directly without going through the skill. Pair it with permissions.ask or permissions.deny rules on the actual deploy commands so the procedure is the only approved path, not merely the only named one.
answers.version_caveat: disable-model-invocation is a Claude Code extension to the Agent Skills standard, not part of the portable spec. In a headless run, --disable-slash-commands turns off all skills and commands, so a CI wrapper would silently lose the entry point. Skills in a plugin are invoked namespaced as /plugin-name:deploy.

answers.primary: A GitHub Action using anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 in a workflow triggered on: issues: types: [opened], with a prompt input describing the triage (label, search for duplicates, post a first response). Supplying prompt puts the action in automation mode, which runs immediately rather than waiting for an @claude mention.
answers.rejected_alternative: A self-hosted headless Agent SDK service reacting to the issues webhook - it gives more control but you rebuild runner provisioning, checkout, token minting and GitHub API plumbing that the action already provides.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness in the broad sense: GitHub Actions decides that the run happens at all, on the webhook event, with no model involvement. The quality of the labelling and duplicate call is the model's, and it is unreviewed.
answers.context_boundary: A fresh, ephemeral context on the GitHub-hosted runner, one per workflow run, sharing nothing with any developer session. In: the issue title and body, repo CLAUDE.md, whatever it queries through the GitHub API. Out: label mutations and a comment, plus the job log.
answers.lifecycle: Starts on the issues.opened webhook and ends when the job finishes, hits --max-turns (default 10) or the workflow timeout. It applies to every new issue from the moment the workflow file merges until it is removed or disabled.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open: a failed or skipped job leaves the issue untriaged and nobody is watching a terminal, so add job-failure alerting. The sharper risk is that issue bodies are attacker-controlled text flowing straight into an agent holding contents/issues/pull-requests write - keep the token scoped, keep --allowedTools tight, and treat mislabelling and false duplicate calls as expected.
answers.version_caveat: v1 is GA and has breaking changes from @beta: mode is removed and auto-detected, direct_prompt became prompt, and max_turns/model/custom_instructions/allowed_tools all moved into claude_args. Needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in repo secrets (or Bedrock/Vertex OIDC with use_bedrock/use_vertex), the Claude GitHub App installed by a repo admin, and contents/issues/pull-requests read-write plus id-token: write for the cloud variants.

answers.primary: An agent team: the main session acts as lead and spawns five teammates, each assigned one hypothesis, instructed to message each other directly and try to disprove the others' theories, with the surviving consensus written to a findings document. This is the documented competing-hypotheses use case for teams.
answers.rejected_alternative: Five Task subagents - they parallelise the investigation but architecturally cannot talk to each other; each only reports back to the main agent, so the adversarial cross-examination you want never happens.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model, at every level. The harness supplies the mailbox files, the shared task list and file-locked task claiming; whether the debate actually happens, and whether the consensus is real rather than premature agreement, is entirely the lead's and teammates' judgement.
answers.context_boundary: Five separate context windows plus the lead's. Each teammate loads CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills fresh but does not inherit the lead's conversation history, so the spawn prompt must carry the case facts. What crosses between them are SendMessage payloads, task-list state and the findings file on disk.
answers.lifecycle: The team forms when the lead spawns the first teammate and is scoped to that one session. Teammates end on shutdown request or session exit; the team config directory is removed automatically at session end while the task list persists under cleanupPeriodDays.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and expensive. Token cost scales roughly linearly with teammate count, the lead often declares consensus before the work is done, teammates sometimes fail to mark tasks complete and block dependents, and a teammate that hits an API error can stop instead of recovering. Note also that a teammate cannot approve a permission prompt for another - relayed approvals are treated as untrusted input.
answers.version_caveat: Experimental and disabled by default: set CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 in settings.json env or the environment, or nothing spawns at all. Behaviour described is v2.1.178+, where TeamCreate/TeamDelete no longer exist and team_name on the Agent tool is ignored. Known limits: one team per session, no nested teams, no restoration of in-process teammates on /resume, and split-pane mode needs tmux or iTerm2 with it2.

answers.primary: A custom output style at .claude/output-styles/data-analyst.md that defines the analyst role and the fixed tabular report format, with keep-coding-instructions left unset so Claude Code's built-in software-engineering instructions are dropped from the system prompt. Select it project-wide by setting outputStyle in .claude/settings.json rather than relying on the /config picker.
answers.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md - it is added as a user message after the system prompt, so it can add analyst conventions but cannot remove the default engineering instructions, which is the explicit requirement here.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness assembles the system prompt and swaps the built-in engineering block out. Actually emitting the tabular format on each reply is the model's job, reinforced by the periodic adherence reminders output styles trigger.
answers.context_boundary: The main conversation's system prompt only. It does not reach subagents, which run their own system prompts; a forked conversation is the exception because it inherits the parent's full system prompt. The added instructions cost input tokens once and are then served from the prompt cache.
answers.lifecycle: Read once at session start and in force for every turn of that session. Changing it takes effect only after /clear or a new session, and it stops applying when the outputStyle setting changes or a plugin style with force-for-plugin overrides it.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory: it is still just system-prompt text, so on long or awkward turns the model drifts out of the strict table shape, and there is no harness check that a reply matched the format. Removing the coding instructions also degrades any incidental engineering work in the project, which is intended here but surprises people who expected a formatting change only.
answers.version_caveat: The standalone /output-style command was deprecated in v2.1.73 and removed in v2.1.91 - use /config or set outputStyle directly. Note that the /config picker writes to .claude/settings.local.json, which is per-developer and not shared, so a project-wide requirement must be committed in .claude/settings.json. As of v2.1.178 nested project output-style directories resolve to the one closest to the working directory.

answers.primary: A headless non-interactive run of the Claude Code CLI (the Agent SDK surface): claude -p with the diff on stdin, pinned with --strict-mcp-config (optionally alongside an explicit --mcp-config), --settings pointing at a settings file committed in the repo, --setting-sources restricted to project, --permission-mode dontAsk and an explicit --allowedTools, with --output-format json for a machine-readable result.
answers.rejected_alternative: The anthropics/claude-code-action GitHub Action - a fine wrapper, but it is a convenience layer over the same headless invocation and does not itself pin away ambient configuration, so you would end up passing the identical isolation flags through claude_args anyway.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Every one of these is a CLI flag evaluated by Claude Code before the model runs; the model cannot re-enable a discarded MCP server or a suppressed user hook from inside the conversation.
answers.context_boundary: A fresh single-turn context per CI run on the runner, sharing nothing with any developer session. In: the diff plus the pinned system prompt and project settings. Out: the JSON result. Add --no-session-persistence so the run leaves no transcript on the runner.
answers.lifecycle: Starts when the CI step executes, ends at the final response or --max-turns / --max-budget-usd. There is no turn boundary in headless mode, so denied actions stay denied for the rest of the run rather than resetting.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed on configuration - --strict-mcp-config discards the project's .mcp.json servers and --bare or --safe-mode also skip auto-discovered hooks, skills, plugins and CLAUDE.md, so a lint pass that quietly depended on one of those just stops working. The bigger caveat is the premise: these flags make the *inputs* identical, not the *output*. Model sampling means byte-for-byte identical text is not something the CLI can promise, so the CI gate should assert on a normalised structured result, not on a diff of the raw reply.
answers.version_caveat: --bare skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md; --safe-mode disables all customisations including workflows and themes - pick whichever matches how much of the project config you actually want. dontAsk mode auto-denies anything not pre-approved and never waits for input, which is the intended CI posture; in -p mode repeated blocks abort the run rather than falling back to prompting. --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections moves machine-specific text out of the system prompt, which also helps runner-to-runner consistency.
